text.en: 536 is called one of the worst years to be alive: volcanic haze dimmed the sun across the Northern Hemisphere, and five years later the Plague of Justinian began.
When Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800, Borobudur — the world's largest Buddhist temple — was being built on Java.
According to the chronicle, the Varangians were invited to Rus' in 862, and in 863 Cyril and Methodius set out for Moravia with a Slavic alphabet.
Rus was baptised in 988, a year after Hugh Capet became King of France. His descendants would rule France for more than 800 years.
The Japanese company Kongō Gumi is older than Islam: it was founded in 578, 44 years before the Hijra — Muhammad's move to Medina, from which the Islamic calendar counts its years.
The Slavic word for 'king' comes from the name Charles — Charlemagne's, or perhaps his great-grandson Charles the Fat's: Latin Karolus became Russian korol', Polish król and Slovak kráľ.

Lowercase Latin letters go back to the handwriting of Charlemagne's scribes. Renaissance humanists found Carolingian minuscule so 'classical' they mistook it for ancient Roman and based their scripts — and later printed type — on it.
Charlemagne had an elephant. Abul-Abbas was a gift from Caliph Harun al-Rashid of Baghdad: shipped to Italy, he crossed the Alps, reached Aachen in 802 and lived at court for eight years.
Charlemagne, patron of a great revival of learning, probably never mastered writing himself. His biographer Einhard says the emperor only tried to learn to write late in life.
In 897 a pope put his predecessor's corpse on trial. Formosus was dug up nine months after his death, robed and propped on a throne, with a deacon answering for him. The verdict: guilty.
Emperor Justinian was nearly overthrown by sports fans. In 532 supporters of the Blue and Green chariot teams dropped their feud, burned half of Constantinople and proclaimed a rival emperor.
Constantinople owes Hagia Sophia to rioting sports fans. The previous church burned in the Nika riots of 532, and Justinian built the present one on its site in just five years.
Hagia Sophia remained the world's largest church for more than 500 years: consecrated in 537, it was surpassed only when the abbey church of Cluny in France was completed in the 12th century.
Byzantine sources claimed that Hagia Sophia's Imperial Gate was made from the timber of Noah's Ark. The seven-metre, 6th-century door was used only by the emperor and his retinue.

During the Nika riots it was his wife who stopped Justinian from fleeing. Empress Theodora, Procopius says, declared that 'royalty is a fine burial shroud'. The emperor stayed — and crushed the revolt.
The secret of silk left Asia inside walking sticks. Around 552 two monks working for Justinian hid silkworm eggs in hollow bamboo canes, and Byzantium began making its own silk.

The recipe for Greek fire was guarded so well that it was lost for good. Byzantium burned enemy fleets with it for seven centuries; today historians can only guess its formula — probably petroleum and resins.
Byzantine emperor Justinian II had his nose cut off in 695 so he could never rule again. In 705 he took back the throne anyway — reputedly wearing a golden nose.
For five centuries nobody knew they were living in AD anything. The monk Dionysius Exiguus devised Anno Domini dating in 525; it caught on thanks to Bede (731) and Charlemagne's court.
There is no year zero because Dionysius Exiguus, inventing AD dating in 525, had no zero. Just 103 years later the Indian Brahmagupta wrote down rules for adding and multiplying with zero.

An 8th-century English king minted a coin bearing the Islamic declaration of faith. Offa of Mercia's gold dinar copies an Abbasid one of 774; the moneyer, knowing no Arabic, set the text upside down and added OFFA REX.

The three-course meal — soup, main, dessert — was reputedly brought to Europe by a Baghdad musician. Ziryab, arriving in Córdoba in 822, set the fashions: haircuts, twice-daily baths, even toothpaste.
The library of Caliph al-Hakam II in Córdoba held an estimated 400,000 to 500,000 volumes. The famous Abbey of Saint Gall at the time had just over a hundred.
The Russian word for China, Kitai, comes from a people who were not Chinese: the nomadic Khitans, who founded the Liao empire in northern China in 916. Medieval Europe made the same name into Cathay.
The name Korea comes from Goryeo, the kingdom founded in 918 that united the peninsula for almost five centuries and under whose name the country became known abroad.
A Chinese emperor took offence at Japan over the sun. In 607 Prince Shōtoku wrote to him: 'The Son of Heaven where the sun rises, to the Son of Heaven where the sun sets.' Emperor Yang was furious.

Japan's holiest shrine has been torn down and rebuilt every 20 years since 692. The current buildings at Ise, from 2013, are the 62nd iteration — so the shrine stays 'forever new and forever ancient'.

A disgraced Japanese minister became the god of learning. Sugawara no Michizane was exiled in 901; after his death disasters struck the capital, and he was deified as Tenjin — to whom students now pray before exams.
In all of Chinese history only one woman ruled as emperor in her own right. Wu Zetian proclaimed her own Zhou dynasty in 690 and even invented new characters, including one for her own name.
Toilet paper is first mentioned in 589, the year the Sui reunited China. The scholar Yan Zhitui wrote that paper bearing quotations from the classics he 'dared not use for toilet purposes'.

Legend says the great Chinese poet Li Bai drowned trying to embrace the moon, leaning drunkenly from his boat towards its reflection in the Yangtze. Other sources point to illness, but the legend endured.
In 763 a Tibetan army captured Chang'an, capital of Tang China and one of the world's largest cities, and installed a puppet emperor. The Tibetans held the city for 15 days.
'Checkmate' is Persian shāh māt, 'the king is helpless'. Around 600 chess reached Sasanian Persia from India as chatrang, and spread from there to the Arabs and Europe.

Medieval tourists in Sri Lanka covered a wall with poems about beauties. On Sigiriya's Mirror Wall scholars read 685 verses from the 8th–10th centuries: men praised the women in the frescoes, women envied them.
The Maya king Pakal took the throne at 12 and ruled for 68 years, from 615 to 683. For over a thousand years no ruler anywhere reigned longer.

A Buddha was dug up in Sweden. On Helgö, an early trading settlement near today's Stockholm, archaeologists found a 6th-century statuette from northern India — alongside an Irish crozier and an Egyptian ladle.
Hagia Sophia has Viking graffiti. On a marble parapet in the upper gallery someone carved the name Halfdan in runes — probably the start of the usual 'Halfdan carved these runes'.

Legend says that when the Viking Rollo received Normandy in 911, he refused to kiss the French king's foot and sent one of his men instead. The warrior lifted the royal foot to his mouth without bending — and the king toppled over.

'Born in the purple' was literal. Legitimate children of Byzantine emperors were born in a palace room faced with purple porphyry, and such sons outranked older brothers born elsewhere in the succession.

Foreign envoys in Constantinople were met by roaring mechanical lions: the 'Throne of Solomon' in the Magnaura hall was said to be ringed by automaton trees with singing birds. The envoy Liutprand, received in 949, left a dazzled account.
Pope Sylvester II's love of mathematics earned him a sorcerer's reputation. He brought the abacus with Hindu-Arabic digits to Europe; legend claimed he won the papacy from the Devil at dice.

The oldest text in French is an oath sworn by a German. In 842 Charlemagne's grandsons swore an alliance: Louis the German in Old French so his brother's soldiers understood, Charles the Bald in Old High German.
The best-known story of Alfred the Great — hiding from the Vikings in 878, he let a peasant woman's cakes burn and got a scolding — is a legend, first written down a century after his death.
The Vikings were not the first in Iceland. Icelandic chronicles say the Norse found Irish hermit monks there — the papar — who left, leaving behind books, bells and croziers.

Japan's oldest surviving tale is about a girl from the Moon. In The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter (late 9th or early 10th century) a tiny Princess Kaguya is found in a glowing bamboo stalk, and in the end returns to the Moon.

The Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan described the Rus as 'tall as date palms'. On the Volga in 922 he admired their build, fair hair and ruddy skin — then called them the filthiest of God's creatures for not even washing their hands after eating.

According to the chronicle, Prince Vladimir rejected Islam over its ban on wine: 'Drinking is the joy of the Rus'. He chose the Greek faith after envoys described a service in Constantinople: 'We knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth.'

Within seven years three great eras began on three sides of the world: in 615 twelve-year-old Pakal became king of Maya Palenque, in 618 the Tang dynasty was founded, and in 622 Muhammad made the Hijra.
The Viking Age and Japan's Heian period began a year apart: Vikings sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne in June 793, and in 794 the Japanese court moved to its new capital, the future Kyoto.

Staraya Ladoga and Baghdad are near-contemporaries and trading partners. Ladoga's oldest buildings date to 753, Baghdad was founded in 762, and by the end of the 8th century Arab silver coins were reaching the Volkhov.
A Japanese inn is older than Rus. Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan has been taking guests since 705 — 157 years before the Varangians were invited to rule — and Guinness lists it as the world's oldest hotel.

The Andromeda Galaxy was first described in 964, a year before Sviatoslav crushed the Khazars. The Persian astronomer al-Sufi called it a 'little cloud'; only in the 20th century did we learn it is another galaxy.
